relationship_to_restored_text: Interpretive contemplative layer aligned by verse. This does not replace the source-audited restored translation.

verses.mystical_translation: A once-powerful king enters bodily dependence; mortality reaches the throne.
The court seeks warmth through a young woman's intimate labor rather than first revealing her voice or choice.
A kingdom-wide search turns Abishag's beauty and body into a royal resource.
She gives care, and the text explicitly denies sexual intercourse while leaving the wider power imbalance unresolved.
Adonijah builds the visual machinery of kingship before receiving communal authorization.
David's failure to question him has helped entitlement grow beside physical attractiveness and birth status.
Military and priestly elites align behind Adonijah.
Other centers of religious, military, and prophetic power remain outside his coalition.
A sacrificial feast gathers family and officials into an emerging regime.
The people most likely to contest the succession are deliberately excluded.
Nathan alerts Bathsheba that power has moved while the aging king remains uninformed.
Counsel becomes a survival practice for a woman and her son under dynastic threat.
Bathsheba is asked to call David back to his promise and expose the competing coronation.
Nathan plans corroboration so her word will not stand alone before royal authority.
Two women occupy the chamber around David: one providing care, one carrying a succession crisis.
Bathsheba must bow before the man whose promise determines whether she and her son survive.
She invokes David's oath in the name of YHWH.
She names the seizure already underway and the king's dangerous unawareness.
The guest list reveals the coalition—and Solomon's exclusion.
The nation waits for a decision concentrated in one aging ruler.
Without public clarity, Bathsheba expects criminalization after David's death.
Nathan arrives while her testimony is still active.
Even the prophet enters through gestures of submission to the throne.
Nathan frames the crisis as a question about whether David secretly authorized it.
Adonijah's feast already performs kingship through abundance, officials, and acclamation.
Nathan inventories those excluded from the new order.
He presses David to disclose whether succession has been arranged without accountable notice.
David recalls Bathsheba into the chamber.
He swears by the life of YHWH and his own history of rescue.
The remembered promise becomes immediate political action.
Bathsheba responds in the required language of royal reverence, even while David is near death.
Priest, prophet, and military executor are summoned to carry the decision.
The king's mule becomes visible proof that Solomon bears David's authority.
Oil, trumpet, and public speech transform a private oath into a coronation.
Solomon is directed toward the throne and rule over both Israel and Judah.
Benaiah seals the command with religious agreement.
The hoped-for future is measured by a throne greater than David's, revealing dynastic ambition inside the blessing.
Royal guards, priest, prophet, and commander escort Solomon into public legitimacy.
Anointing and trumpet call draw the people into the new kingship.
Popular joy becomes so loud the earth seems to break.
The rival feast hears that power has shifted elsewhere.
Adonijah mistakes the messenger's character for assurance that news will favor him.
Jonathan answers with the unwelcome reality: David has crowned Solomon.
Every royal symbol confirms the transfer.
The city's rejoicing announces that Adonijah's private coalition has lost the public center.
Solomon now occupies the throne.
Servants bless the new dynasty while David bows from his bed.
David gives thanks that he has lived to see succession.
Adonijah's guests scatter when patronage becomes liability.
The would-be king becomes a frightened sanctuary seeker.
He asks for an oath against execution because his life now depends on his rival's discretion.
Solomon offers conditional safety while retaining the right to define future evil.
Adonijah bows and is sent home, but the threat beneath the settlement remains.

contemplative_note: The chapter asks who pays for succession: an aging body, a young caregiver, a politically endangered mother, excluded officials, animals, servants, and a frightened rival. Sacred symbols may legitimate power, but they do not answer whether power is just.
